## Principle
Heat exchangers are widely used in the process industries, across a wide range of applications, from heating and cooling process streams to the recovery of heat that would otherwise be wasted. A heat exchanger is a device in which heat is transferred from a hotter fluid to a colder fluid through a solid wall, with the two fluids remaining physically separate throughout the process. A sound understanding of how this transfer takes place, and of the factors that govern its rate, is fundamental to the design and the operation of a very large proportion of process plant.

The driving force for heat transfer in an exchanger is the temperature difference between the two streams. Wherever a temperature difference exists between the hot stream and the cold stream, heat flows from the hotter stream to the colder stream, and the local rate at which it flows is proportional to the local temperature difference. It is important to appreciate, however, that this temperature difference is by no means constant along the length of the exchanger: the hot stream cools as it gives up heat, the cold stream warms as it receives heat, and the difference between them therefore changes continuously from one end of the exchanger to the other. This gradual variation is one of the main reasons why the analysis of heat exchangers calls for some care, and why a simple average of the end temperature differences is, in general, not an adequate basis for design calculations.

When the overall rate of heat transfer is under consideration, it is conventionally expressed through an overall heat transfer coefficient, which conveniently brings together the resistances to heat transfer on the hot side, through the wall, and on the cold side. These resistances act in series with one another, and the largest of them will tend to dominate the overall behaviour of the unit. It is also worth noting that fouling, in which deposits build up gradually on the heat transfer surfaces during service, can add a further resistance that may become significant over time. Because of this, the performance of an exchanger in day-to-day operation may differ appreciably from its performance when new and clean, and this needs to be borne in mind when operating behaviour is interpreted.

The two streams can be arranged in a number of different flow configurations, and the chosen configuration has an important influence both on the temperature profiles within the exchanger and on how closely the outlet temperature of one stream can be brought towards the inlet temperature of the other. In co-current flow the two streams enter at the same end and move through the exchanger in the same direction, so that the temperature difference is largest at the inlet end and falls steadily along the length. In countercurrent flow, by contrast, the streams enter at opposite ends and move towards one another, and the temperature difference is that much more even along the length. As the worked example later in this chapter shows, the countercurrent arrangement is generally to be preferred wherever the mechanical design allows it, because it makes better overall use of the available temperature difference.

## Equipment
A range of exchanger constructions is in common use, and the choice between them depends on the duties involved, the pressures and temperatures to be handled, the corrosiveness and fouling tendency of the fluids, and, of course, on cost. The most familiar construction is probably the shell-and-tube exchanger, in which one fluid flows through a bundle of tubes while the other flows across and along those tubes within a surrounding shell. Baffles inside the shell direct this second stream backwards and forwards across the tube bundle, which improves heat transfer and also supports the tubes. Shell-and-tube units are robust, they can be built for very high pressures, and individual tubes can be cleaned or replaced.

Plate exchangers offer an alternative construction in which thin corrugated plates are clamped together in a frame, with the two fluids flowing in the narrow passages between alternate plates. Units of this kind provide a large surface area in a compact volume and achieve high coefficients, although the gaskets between the plates place limits on the pressures and temperatures, and the narrow passages are prone to blockage where the fluids contain solids. Double-pipe exchangers, in which one pipe is simply mounted inside another, are the simplest construction of all and remain useful for small duties, for high pressures, and for teaching and test work. Other constructions, including spiral and air-cooled exchangers, meet more specialised needs.

## Worked example
To see how the ideas developed above are applied in practice, consider a countercurrent shell-and-tube exchanger in which a hot process stream is cooled by a cold utility stream. The quantities that characterise the problem are the temperatures at which the two streams enter and leave the exchanger, and these are the values set out in the principle section of this chapter, where the temperature difference between the streams was discussed; no additional data are needed for the calculation that follows, and none are introduced. In the first step of the calculation, the temperature differences between the streams at the two ends of the exchanger are obtained by subtracting, at each end, the cold stream temperature from the hot stream temperature at that same end. Because the arrangement is countercurrent, care has to be taken at this point to pair each hot stream temperature with the cold stream temperature at the same physical end of the exchanger, and not with the temperature at the opposite end, an easily made mistake with a seriously misleading result.

The next step is to combine these two end differences into the logarithmic mean temperature difference, which is the appropriate average driving force for an exchanger in which the temperature difference varies along the length in the manner described earlier. The logarithmic mean is found from the two end differences through the standard logarithmic-mean relation, and it always lies between them, closer to the smaller of the two. Finally, the required heat transfer area is obtained by dividing the duty of the exchanger by the product of the overall heat transfer coefficient and this logarithmic mean temperature difference. The result of the calculation can be checked in a straightforward qualitative way: where the two end differences are close to one another, the logarithmic mean should be close to both of them, and where they differ widely, the mean should sit well below the arithmetic average of the two, and a result that fails either of these checks has almost certainly been obtained by pairing the temperatures incorrectly or by averaging in the wrong way.

## Limits
The simple model used in this chapter rests on a number of assumptions, and it is important to be clear about where those assumptions cease to be a good description of a real exchanger. The overall heat transfer coefficient has been treated as a constant along the whole length of the exchanger, whereas in practice it varies as the fluid properties change with temperature, and it may vary quite markedly where a stream is close to a change of state. The model also assumes that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, which is a reasonable approximation for a well-insulated industrial unit but a poor one for small or uninsulated equipment. Phase change has been excluded throughout, although condensation and boiling are common industrial operations and require a different treatment of the coefficients on the side where the change occurs. Finally, fouling has been mentioned as an added resistance, but the simple model takes no account of the way a fouling layer grows with time in service, so it cannot predict how performance will decline between one cleaning and the next. Within these limits, the model is a dependable tool for sizing and for rating straightforward exchangers; outside them, more detailed methods are needed.

## Principle
A heat exchanger transfers heat from a hotter fluid to a colder fluid through a solid wall, with the two fluids physically separate. Heat exchangers heat and cool process streams and recover heat that would otherwise leave the process unused, and the rate at which an exchanger transfers heat governs the sizing of much of the plant around it.

The temperature difference between the two streams is the driving force for the transfer. Heat flows from the hotter stream to the colder stream, and the local rate is proportional to the local temperature difference. The difference is not constant along the exchanger: the hot stream cools as it gives up heat and the cold stream warms as it receives heat, so the difference changes continuously from one end to the other. A simple average of the end differences is therefore not an adequate basis for design, and the variation has to be carried through the calculation.

The overall rate is expressed through an overall heat transfer coefficient, which combines the resistances on the hot side, through the wall, and on the cold side. The resistances act in series, and the largest dominates the overall behaviour. Fouling adds a further resistance: deposits build up on the heat transfer surfaces in service, and an exchanger that performs well when clean may perform appreciably worse after a period in operation. Performance in service is interpreted against that growth, not against the clean condition.

The flow configuration sets the temperature profiles and the closest approach between the outlet temperature of one stream and the inlet temperature of the other. In co-current flow the streams enter at the same end and move in the same direction, and the temperature difference is largest at the inlet end and falls along the length. In countercurrent flow the streams enter at opposite ends and move towards one another, and the difference is more even along the length. Countercurrent flow is preferred where the mechanical design allows it, because it makes better use of the available temperature difference, as the worked example in this chapter shows. The same quantities recur throughout the chapter, and each is used in the sense fixed where it first appears.

## Equipment
Exchanger constructions differ in the duties they suit, the pressures and temperatures they withstand, and their tolerance of corrosive and fouling fluids. The shell-and-tube exchanger is the most familiar construction: one fluid flows through a bundle of tubes and the other flows across and along the tubes inside a surrounding shell. Baffles in the shell direct the shell-side stream backwards and forwards across the bundle, which improves heat transfer and supports the tubes. Shell-and-tube units are robust, can be built for high pressures, and allow individual tubes to be cleaned or replaced.

Plate exchangers clamp thin corrugated plates together in a frame, with the two fluids in the narrow passages between alternate plates. The construction gives a large surface area in a compact volume and high coefficients. Gaskets between the plates limit the pressures and temperatures the unit can handle, and the narrow passages block where a fluid contains solids. A double-pipe exchanger, one pipe mounted inside another, is the simplest construction and serves small duties, high pressures, and test work. Spiral and air-cooled exchangers meet more specialised needs. Every construction works on the principle set out in the previous section: heat passes from the hotter stream to the colder stream through a separating wall, at a rate set by the temperature difference and the resistances in series.

## Worked example
A countercurrent shell-and-tube exchanger cools a hot process stream with a cold utility stream. The calculation uses the stream temperatures at entry and exit set out in the principle section of this chapter; no further data are required and none are introduced. The first step obtains the temperature difference at each end of the exchanger, subtracting the cold stream temperature from the hot stream temperature at the same end. In countercurrent flow the pairing is the step at risk: each hot stream temperature belongs with the cold stream temperature at the same physical end, and pairing across the ends gives a seriously misleading driving force.

The two end differences are combined into the logarithmic mean temperature difference, the average driving force for an exchanger whose temperature difference varies along its length. The logarithmic mean is calculated from the two end differences by the logarithmic-mean relation; it lies between them, closer to the smaller. The required heat transfer area is then obtained by dividing the duty by the product of the overall heat transfer coefficient and the logarithmic mean temperature difference. A qualitative check closes the calculation: where the end differences are close, the logarithmic mean stands close to both; where they differ widely, the mean stands well below their arithmetic average. A result that fails the check points to a pairing error or to the wrong average.

## Limits
The model in this chapter treats the overall heat transfer coefficient as constant along the exchanger. Fluid properties change with temperature, so the coefficient varies along the length in practice, and the variation is marked where a stream approaches a change of state. The model also takes the exchanger as exchanging no heat with its surroundings, an approximation that holds for a well-insulated industrial unit and fails for small or uninsulated equipment. Phase change is excluded throughout: condensation and boiling are common industrial operations, and the side on which the change occurs needs a different treatment of its coefficient. Fouling enters the model only as an added resistance at a stated condition; the growth of a fouling layer with time in service is not represented, so the model cannot predict the decline in performance between cleanings. Within these limits the model sizes and rates straightforward exchangers dependably, and the quantities and checks of this chapter remain the starting point for the more detailed methods that the excluded cases require. The worked example stays inside these limits deliberately, so that each step of the calculation can be followed without the qualifications competing with the method being taught.
